title: Why Doing Two Things at Once Breaks Everything
subtitle: Run two bits of code at the same time and they can trip over each other in ways that vanish the moment you look. Welcome to concurrency.
hook: You'd think doing two things at once is just… faster. But let two programs touch the same data at the same moment and you get bugs that are maddening: they appear randomly, vanish when you add a print statement, and can't be reproduced on demand. This is **concurrency**, the part of software that humbles everyone. Today: why it's so hard, and the one idea that tames it.

sections.heading: The race condition
sections.body:
Say your bank balance is $100 and two withdrawals of $100 hit at the exact same instant. Each one reads the balance ($100 — enough!), each approves, each subtracts. You've now withdrawn $200 from $100. Nobody wrote a bug; the *interleaving* did it.

That's a **race condition**: the result depends on the unpredictable order in which concurrent operations run. Because timing shifts run to run, the bug is a ghost — which is what makes it so nasty.

sections.caption: Two withdrawals interleave: both read $100 before either writes. The lost update is nobody's 'mistake' — it's the ordering.

sections.label: The fix: make it atomic
sections.body: The cure is to protect the shared data so only one operation touches it at a time — a **lock** (or 'mutex'). Whoever grabs the lock finishes their read-decide-write as one indivisible ("atomic") step before anyone else gets in. But locks bring their own demons: hold too many and two threads can each wait forever for the other — a **deadlock**. Concurrency is the art of sharing safely without freezing up.

sections.label: Why it matters everywhere
sections.body: Every database, web server, and multi-core app juggles concurrent work. It's why your money doesn't (usually) double-spend and why 'just add threads to go faster' often makes things slower and buggier. The hardest bugs in production are almost always concurrency bugs.

sections.caption: Threads, locks, deadlocks, and race conditions — the whole concurrency zoo in one tour.

takeaways: Running things at once introduces **race conditions** — results that depend on timing.
Classic example: two operations both read stale data before either writes (lost update).
**Locks/mutexes** make a read-modify-write **atomic** so only one goes at a time.
Locks risk **deadlock** — threads waiting on each other forever.
Concurrency bugs are the hardest in production: rare, random, and hard to reproduce.

options: A bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of concurrent operations
quiz.explain: The 'race' is between operations; who finishes first changes the result.

options: Lets only one operation touch shared data at a time (atomicity)
quiz.explain: It serializes access so a read-modify-write can't be interrupted mid-way.

quiz.q: BOSS: You add locks everywhere to be safe, and now the app sometimes freezes completely. Likely cause?
options: Deadlock — threads each holding a lock the other needs, waiting forever
quiz.explain: Over-locking trades race conditions for deadlocks. Safe concurrency is about locking the *right* things, minimally.

tg_quiz.q: Two $100 withdrawals hit a $100 balance at once, both read before either writes. Result?
tg_quiz.correct: Exactly — that's a race condition (lost update).
tg_quiz.wrong: Both read $100 first, so both approve — $200 out. That's a race condition.
tg_quiz.explain: A lock makes the read-decide-write atomic so this can't happen.
